about_us_meta_desc: Project Bruut is by and for the community: an open-source field robot that farmers and makers can build, understand and adapt themselves.
about_us_intro: Robotics in agriculture is often complex and unaffordable. We believe this can be different. Bruut is a modular, open-source field robot that you, as a farmer or maker, can build, understand and adapt yourself.
about_us_photo_alt: The robot frame in the workshop, with both steering heads
about_us_opensource_text: You are not locked into expensive licences or closed systems. You adapt the tool carrier to your own work and share your improvements with others.
about_us_independence_text: No unnecessary electronics. As many standard off-the-shelf parts as possible, so you repair the robot yourself in the field without waiting for a mechanic.
about_us_reality_text: Robotics is hard. Do not expect a ready-made product with a bow on top. Do expect a robust, programmable frame and a clear manual. We provide the tools, you give the robot its purpose.
about_us_community_text: Whether you are a farmer with a welder or a developer who likes working with ArduPilot: we do this together. Sharing ideas, improving them, testing in the mud and using them together.
about_us_conclusion: Help build accessible agricultural robotics. Share your implements, improve the code or start building your own Bruut.

front_page_origin_p2: After computer vision in the barn came the step into robotics: a simple field robot for less chemistry, lower fuel and machinery costs and less heavy work. Spot spraying, mechanical weeding and better soil health come first.

func_meta_desc: All implements and applications for the Bruut field robot, from overseeder to wildlife deterrent. Five implements are fully worked out in FreeCAD, with calculations and animations.
func_hero_subtitle: Bruut is a tool carrier: the frame stays, the work changes. These are all implements and applications for the field, the greenhouse and the yard.
func_hero_alt: The liquid fertilizer applicator behind the robot, as a FreeCAD model
func_featured_title: Worked out down to the bolt
func_featured_desc: These five implements are designed parametrically in FreeCAD, with calculations, drawings and animations on the robot.
func_grass_meter_alt: The prototype with a grass height meter in the field
func_1_desc: Front-mounted or mid-mounted between the front and rear wheels. Usable as a grader for leveling terrain, for pushing feed and grass back in the stable, or for cleaning silos.
func_2_desc: Trencher for digging wet buffer strips and drainage ditches, so standing water is carried off the field efficiently.
func_3_desc: Compact cultivator for soil cultivation in vegetable gardens and light plots.
func_4_desc: Hoeing unit with single-axis (left/right) guidance that stays tightly between the rows, for example in maize, so weeds are cut close to the crop without damaging it.
func_5_desc: Mechanical weed control using rotating fingers in light soil.
func_6_desc: Front-mounted boom with conventional high-pressure nozzles that atomise the liquid into a fine mist. Each nozzle is switched individually, so only the detected weed is treated while the fine droplets fully cover the leaf surface. Based on the 'Open Weed Locator' project and ideal for contact herbicides and crop protection products.
func_7_desc: Boom with individually controlled injectors that fire single coarse droplets on demand at low pressure. Every droplet is placed straight onto the weed, which practically eliminates drift and cuts chemical usage to a fraction of a conventional spray pass.
func_8_desc: Two-axis system with CNC movement (left/right and up/down) carrying a drill that grinds individual weeds out of the sward. Developed for tap-rooted weeds such as broad-leaved dock, fully chemical-free.
func_9_desc: Improving soil structure and air supply in grassland.
func_10_desc: Mowing at various heights, including 'topping' plants above ground level.
func_11_desc: Flexible arm with a brush cutter head or blades for mowing under fences and around obstacles.
func_12_desc: Pumping water from ditches for local irrigation or crop spraying.
func_13_desc: Precise application and spreading of granular fertilizers.
func_14_desc: Spreading lime to improve soil pH levels and structure.
func_15_desc: Seed box for initial crop sowing and for overseeding existing grassland in one pass.
func_16_desc: Front-mounted unit that takes seedlings out of the tray and sets them out at the right spacing.
func_17_desc: Compact seeder that spreads grass seed onto bare patches in the sward, so damaged spots close up again quickly.
func_18_desc: Even distribution of sawdust or bedding material in stables.
func_19_desc: Evenly spreading straw, specially designed for use between vegetable rows.
func_20_desc: Transporting compost within the frame structure and spreading it between the crop rows.
func_21_desc: Additional power supply modules to be installed between the frames.
func_22_desc: Generator or combustion engine mounted between the frame as an auxiliary power source for extra electricity or mechanical power.
func_23_desc: Integrated panels to extend battery life and provide sustainable power during operation.
func_24_desc: Electric motors such as the Ego Power+ or Greenworks units to drive implements that need real power, replacing small petrol engines.
func_25_desc: Large front-mounted brush or electrically driven radial brush for surface cleaning, as an alternative to the front push blade.
func_26_desc: Front or rear-mounted seat, with the option to widen the frame tubes at the sides.
func_27_desc: Motorized wheelbarrow-style bin for transporting and dumping loose materials, also usable as a carrying aid or mini dumper.
func_28_desc: Rear-mounted hitch for pulling trailers and other rolling equipment.
func_29_desc: Ballast weights to improve traction and vehicle balance for heavy tasks.
func_30_desc: External hydraulic power source for applications where hydraulics are a better option than electricity.
func_31_desc: Standard lifting system for attaching various agricultural implements.
func_32_desc: Protective enclosure or housing for the operator.
func_33_desc: Measuring grass and crop height and health to create task maps for nitrogen or phosphate.
func_34_desc: Measuring and mapping soil density at specific data points.
func_35_desc: Near-infrared sensor that measures the NDVI of the crop while driving. From the difference between reflected red and near-infrared light the robot reads biomass, ground cover and crop vitality, and builds live task maps for variable-rate fertilisation. Because the sensor moves close over the crop instead of looking down from a satellite, the readings stay reliable under cloud cover and also register small spots and gaps.
func_36_desc: The robot works together with a drone as a mobile base station. The drone flies out from the platform, maps the plot from above and passes its imagery straight to the robot, which converts it into a driving and treatment plan. The drone charges and swaps batteries on the robot, so the pair can keep scouting and working alternately for a full day without anyone coming out to the field.
func_37_desc: Several Bruut units work the same field as one swarm. The job is split into sections, the robots divide the passes among themselves and keep each other informed of position, progress and battery state, so they never overlap or cross. Capacity scales simply with the number of units instead of with machine size, work continues when one unit drops out, and the light platforms keep soil compaction low.
func_38_desc: Dosing unit for liquid fertiliser, built for RENURE: mineral nitrogen recovered from animal manure, which the EU allows as a replacement for fossil fertiliser. This closes the nutrient cycle on the farm or in the region and reduces the need for fertiliser whose production uses a lot of natural gas. The robot works from task maps made by the grass meter, NIR sensor or drone and adjusts the rate per square metre. Where the crop lags behind it gets more, and where there is already enough nitrogen nothing is applied. The liquid goes into the sward just above the ground, with no mist or drift, and a light robot can drive when the land is too wet for a tractor with a tank. Every application is logged with its GPS position, which makes fertiliser record-keeping easier.
func_39_desc: Trailer with a pop-up tent that serves as a mobile shed for the robot. The trailer carries the robot by road from field to field, or stays parked at the edge of the plot so the robot can spend the night there, dry and out of sight. From the tent the robot starts its task remotely, so the farmer does not have to drive out and unload it first.
func_40_desc: Fixed charging point at the edge of the field, like the one a robotic lawn mower uses. When the battery runs low, the robot drives to the station by itself, docks, recharges and then carries on from where it left off. Large plots are finished over several rounds without anyone having to fetch the robot or plug it in.
func_41_desc: In Cycly mode the robot stays on one plot for a longer period. Every few days it runs a weeder harrow over the field to remove weeds at the seedling stage, before they can take hold. It uses the weather forecast to pick the dry spells between showers, so it does not smear the soil. In between it recharges at the charging station or in the trailer. Through the cameras the farmer keeps an eye on the crop and the robot remotely, without having to go out to the field.
func_42_desc: When spreading fertiliser or sowing, the robot drives to a supply hopper on the headland once its bin is empty and refills automatically. It then returns to the spot where it stopped and continues the pass. This way a small, light platform can still cover a large plot, with nobody needed on site to top it up.
func_43_desc: The robot as a mobile wildlife deterrent, with a 360-degree camera and solar panels so it can stay out in the field day and night. It moves along with your livestock in the pasture, or drives a set patrol around the plot to keep geese, wild boar or wolves at bay. Using AI it recognises the animals on the camera feed and learns from earlier visits when and where they usually turn up, so it is already there before the damage is done. When wildlife comes into view it scares the animals off with sound and light, and the farmer gets an alert on their phone straight away. Because the robot keeps changing position and varies its deterrent each time, animals get used to it far less quickly than to a fixed bird banger or scarecrow.
func_44_desc: Through a belt or chain drive that turns with the robot's travel, it can power existing mechanically driven implements, such as a small ELHO tedder or rake. The rotating parts of the implement run in step with the driving speed, just like the old ground-driven machines behind a horse or tractor. The implement itself needs no separate motor, electronics or hydraulics, giving simple, robust and often second-hand machines a second life behind an autonomous robot.
impl_calcs_desc: From the calculation scripts in the repository. They read the same parameters as the 3D model, so a different dimension gives different numbers straight away.
impl_cta_desc: All files are open on GitHub: the FreeCAD model, STEP export, calculation scripts and the reasoning behind every dimension.
goal_meta_desc: Why Bruut exists: making agricultural robotics accessible with an open, simple base that farmers and makers build, share and improve themselves.
goal_hero_subtitle: Making complex robotics accessible by providing a solid base, driven by an active community of farmers and makers.
goal_story_title: From base frame to your own application
goal_story_desc: We provide the tools and the setup. The farmer or maker gives it a purpose.
goal_story_1_desc: Box beams with a hole pattern on four wheel units. Wider, longer or higher without welding.
goal_story_1_alt: The bare frame on four wheel units in the workshop
goal_story_2_desc: Add battery, control and RTK, and the robot drives into the field on its own.
goal_story_2_alt: The prototype with a seat and a grass height meter in the field
goal_story_3_desc: An implement you choose, share or design yourself. Like this overseeder.
goal_story_3_alt: Overseeder behind the robot, as a FreeCAD model
goal_problem_1_desc: Spot spraying only hits the weed. Mechanical weeding and the dock weed mill sometimes make chemicals unnecessary altogether.
goal_problem_2_desc: Electric and light: no diesel, little maintenance and parts you replace yourself. From about €6,000 in parts.
goal_problem_3_desc: The robot can take over pushing feed, hoeing and scouting, even when no staff can be found.
goal_problem_4_desc: About 1 kg/cm² ground pressure at 0.8 bar, and the option to work with several small robots instead of one heavy machine.
goal_feature1_desc: A platform where makers and enthusiasts share, improve and test their designs, code and attachments.
goal_feature2_desc: With electric drive and solar panel options, the robot is ideal for zero-emission work in greenhouses and in the field.
goal_feature3_desc: Lighter and more efficient work for agricultural entrepreneurs, from large-scale farming to small vegetable gardens.
goal_cta_desc: Follow the build, ask questions or contribute your own implement. Everything happens in the open.
robotbuild_meta_desc: Build your own Bruut field robot: hole-grid frame, wheel units with hub motor, steering heads with stepper motor. With FreeCAD model, drawings and four versions.
robotbuild_hero_subtitle: A frame of box-section beams with a hole pattern, four wheel units and standard electronics. All drawings and models are open on GitHub.
robotbuild_prototype_alt: A team member next to the Bruut prototype with a seat in a grass field
robotbuild_workshop_desc: Everything on this page has really been built and driven. The electronics are deliberately still visible, so everything can be rebuilt, re-measured or rewired between two test drives.
robotbuild_photo_1: The frame on four wheel units, from the front
robotbuild_photo_2: Steering head with stepper motor above the front wheel
robotbuild_photo_3: Side view: box beams on the wheel brackets
robotbuild_photo_4: From above: the hole pattern in the box beams
robotbuild_photo_5: Both steering heads, with the GNSS antenna between them
robotbuild_cad_desc: The model is rebuilt from the OpenSCAD files and the photos of the prototype. Every dimension lives in one parameter file: change it and the whole model is rebuilt.
robotbuild_steer_desc: Each front wheel turns on its own steering shaft with a NEMA 34 and a 5:1 planetary gearbox. The inner wheel steers sharper than the outer: at 25° centre angle 29.5° against 21.6°.
robotbuild_frame_desc: Box beams with a continuous hole pattern. You set track width and wheelbase by bolting the beams into a different row of holes, without welding.
robotbuild_wheelunit_desc: One hub motor, two side plates and a top plate with slotted holes. The unit bolts to the frame as one module: swapping a motor takes minutes.
robotbuild_steerhead_desc: Two flange bearings in plates below and above the frame, a Ø 25 mm steering shaft and the stepper motor on top.
robotbuild_maintenance_desc: 60 V maximum, a main switch and a clearly visible emergency stop. Removable power tool battery packs and electronics in accessible boxes.
robotbuild_laser_label: Laser cutting for all four wheel modules, incl. VAT
robotbuild_laser_desc: 8 side plates, 8 axle brackets and 4 top plates. All drawings are in the repository, so any sheet metal shop can make them.
robotbuild_versions_desc: The Agbot XL has 16-inch hub motors, 200/70R16 tyres and 60 mm box beams. The same software, a different size.
robotbuild_compare_side: Side view at the same scale, with a 1.80 m person.
robotbuild_compare_top: Top view, grid lines every 500 mm.
robotbuild_compare_video: Both robots drive the same turn. The XL has a 40% larger turning radius.
robotbuild_progress_desc: This is where the project stands today. Every step, including the ones that went wrong, is on the YouTube channel.
robotbuild_steering_desc: The robot started as a differential-drive two-wheeler, but accurate line following was hard to tune. Now it steers like a tricycle with a pure pursuit algorithm that keeps it on its path.
robotbuild_ardupilot_desc: For RTK and autonomous driving we build on ArduPilot. The robot drives missions between AB points on its own; line following does not yet work on every surface and in every turn.
robotbuild_vision_desc: A global shutter camera gives no skewed images while driving. With SAHI (sliced inference) small objects such as young plants are recognised noticeably better.
robotbuild_steppers_desc: Implements need to move sideways and up and down. NEMA 34 stepper motors have enough torque for a side-shift frame and are easy to control.
robotbuild_spot_spraying_desc: Spot spraying builds on the open-source Open Weed Locator (OWL). Innovators like Guy Coleman show the open-source community at its best.
robotbuild_inrow_desc: Computer vision decides which plant stays. There are working tests for hoeing between cauliflower, side-shift hoeing and recognising spindle trees in the row.
robotbuild_videos_cta_desc: Every build step, test drive and setback is filmed and explained. A new video appears on the channel every few weeks.
robotbuild_play_video: Play the video: the robot in action
timeline_hubmotor_body: The project starts with a single 48V hub motor on the workbench. Does it turn, how much force does it have, and can it be controlled finely enough for a field robot? Everything that follows is built on the answer to that question.
timeline_arduino_body: Through a DAC module an Arduino drives the throttle input of the motor controller. Speed is now set by software instead of by a physical dial. This is the step from electric to controllable.
timeline_twowheels_body: Two hub motors now run together from the same Arduino. Running the left wheel faster than the right makes the robot turn, without a single moving steering part. That differential steering stays Bruut's way of turning corners for months.
timeline_rover_body: Motors, brackets and a simple frame have come together into a rolling rover. For the first time the project moves across the ground instead of across the workbench. Not a field robot yet, but proof that the drivetrain is sound.
timeline_remote_body: The rover gets a remote control so it can be steered from the sidelines. That is what makes outdoor testing practical: you can correct before something goes wrong. It is also the stepping stone to autonomy, because software can later issue those same steering commands.
timeline_firstfield_title: Into the field for the first time
timeline_firstfield_body: The first test run on real ground instead of the yard. Holes, grass and loose surfaces do something very different to a robot than a flat floor. From here on every step is tested in the field, not just thought through indoors.
timeline_rtk_body: The ArduSimple RTK receiver makes its first connection and delivers centimetre-level positioning. Ordinary GPS is metres off, which makes it useless between crop rows. This connection is the precondition for everything that later has to drive straight on its own.
timeline_codebase_title: New codebase and the first images
timeline_codebase_body: The control software moves to a new codebase in Svelte, with a browser-based operating screen. At the same time the first computer vision arrives: the robot no longer looks only at coordinates, but at what it sees. Software and camera are developed together from now on.
timeline_taskmaps_body: What the camera detects is translated into a task map of the field. That way the robot knows not only where it is, but where there is work to do. Detecting and acting come together in one system for the first time.
timeline_waypoints_body: The robot drives from waypoint to waypoint on its own, with nobody touching the transmitter. RTK position, heading and control work as a single whole here for the first time. This is the day Bruut goes from remote-controlled to autonomous.
timeline_cropmodel_title: The first model that recognises crops
timeline_cropmodel_body: A trained model recognises cauliflower plants in the row and turns them into a visualisation of where hoeing is allowed. Telling weeds and crops apart is exactly the hard part of mechanical hoeing. This is the first AI model that understands the field.
timeline_heading_title: The robot knows which way it faces
timeline_heading_body: Besides a position, the robot now has a reliable heading. Without heading you know where you are, but not which way to steer to get somewhere. With this addition, corners and lining up on a track become far calmer.
timeline_rain_title: Rained on: one step forward, two back
timeline_rain_body: A rain shower reaches the electronics and puts the robot out of action. Working outdoors means water, dust and vibration, and the build has to survive all three. The lesson from this day is baked into every enclosure and cable run that follows.
timeline_hoeing_body: Computer vision and drivetrain come together in a proof of concept: driving the row and hoeing based on what the camera sees. It is not yet an implement that lasts a full day, but it shows the idea works. From here the goal is no longer just driving, but getting work done.
timeline_tricycle_body: Steering on speed difference drags the wheels across the ground and is imprecise at low speed. So the design switches to tricycle steering, with a properly steered wheel. It drives more calmly, tracks better and suits precise work in the row far more.
timeline_purepursuitfirst_body: The robot drives a mission along AB points using the Pure Pursuit algorithm. Instead of steering at a single target, it keeps aiming at a point ahead on the line. That makes it weave less and follow the route far more smoothly.
timeline_globalshutter_body: The field robot gets a global shutter camera instead of a rolling shutter one. It captures the whole frame at once, so images taken while driving no longer skew. For detection at speed that directly improves reliability.
timeline_design_body: One long video puts every design choice for the real Bruut on the table: modular, electric, and buildable with ordinary workshop tools. Everything learned on the prototype is folded into this design. Construction of the definitive machine starts right after.
timeline_lasercut_body: The CAD drawings went to the laser cutter and came back as real sheet metal parts. That turned Bruut from a 3D model into a machine you can actually pick up. Every part is deliberately flat and simple, so anyone can have them cut locally.
timeline_wheelmodules_body: The laser-cut plates were welded together into complete wheel modules around a 48V hub motor. That module is the heart of the modular idea: the same unit fits on every corner of the robot. Want 2WD or 4WD? Simply build the same thing two or four times.
timeline_chassis_body: The tubes were drilled to size and the frame was bolted together for the first time. From this point on Bruut has a real load-bearing frame instead of a pile of loose parts. Because the joints are bolted, the frame stays adjustable later without reaching for an angle grinder.
timeline_hubmotors_body: The wheel modules with hub motors were slid under the iron frame and fixed in place. For the first time the new robot stands on its own four wheels on the ground. The drive sits inside the wheel itself, so no gearbox or chain is needed.
timeline_electronics_body: Batteries, controllers and wiring were installed and explained step by step in the video. This gave the frame its first power and a central nervous system. The layout is deliberately kept readable, so you can rebuild it and extend it yourself.
timeline_firstdrive_title: First metres on the iron frame
timeline_firstdrive_body: With the motors driven, the new machine covered its very first metres. That proved the drivetrain, power supply and controls work together in this build too. From here the focus shifted from building back to controlling.
timeline_casters_body: The rear caster wheels looked like a simple solution but turned out to be unpredictable in the field. While turning they fought back and pulled the robot off course. This failure was the deciding argument for switching to properly steered wheels.
timeline_steering_body: Two wheels each got their own stepper motor, so the steering angle can be set degree by degree. The robot's heading is now controlled purely digitally, without a mechanical steering link. This is the foundation every autonomous function relies on afterwards.
timeline_autonomous_body: With nobody touching the transmitter, the new machine also drives to a given point on its own. It picks its own heading, corrects along the way and stops at the destination. Everything learned on the prototype now works on the definitive robot.
timeline_purepursuit_body: In one uncut recording the robot completes a full Pure Pursuit mission. Nothing is edited out, so the corrections and the hesitations are visible too. No longer a few metres, but an entire route from start to finish.
timeline_precision_body: While driving AB lines the deviation stays around six centimetres on average. That order of magnitude is exactly what you need to work between crop rows later on. There is still room to improve, but the track is usable now rather than merely indicative.
timeline_speed6_body: The AB line is now followed at 6 km/h instead of walking pace. Higher speed puts sharper demands on the controller, because errors build up faster. The track staying tight anyway shows the steering has margin left for real field work.
timeline_spraybar_body: With driving under control, attention shifts to the implements behind the robot. The choice falls on a coarse-droplet spray boom instead of a misting one. Coarse droplets drift far less and suit precise driving along fixed lines.
timeline_dock_body: A concept for autonomously drilling out broad-leaved dock instead of spraying it. The plant is recognised, driven up to and dealt with mechanically, without treating the whole field. Together with the grass meter, this is the direction the implement range is heading.
timeline_grassheight_body: The robot measures grass height at points and estimates what sits between those points. That produces a picture of the whole field instead of isolated readings. It turns the field robot into a measuring instrument for grassland management as well.
